segments.text: This is a short story. It's called The Vending Machine That Only Sells Apologies.
There's a vending machine on the third floor of the Holloway Street parking garage,
between the stairwell and the broken elevator, and it only sells apologies. Nobody installed it.
The building manager, a tired man named Petrosyan, checked.
There's no invoice, no service contract, and no plug. It just hums.
The buttons are labelled the way buttons always are, A1 through F6, but behind the glass,
instead of crisps and chocolate, there are small paper envelopes, each one the size of a business card.
A1 costs a quarter. F6 costs eleven dollars and forty cents.
The first person to use it was a nurse coming off a night shift.
She'd had a bad week, and she put in a quarter mostly out of spite, and pressed A1.
The envelope dropped.
Inside, in neat handwriting, it said, sorry about the parking ticket, that one was a mistake.
She laughed out loud in the empty garage.
And the next morning, there was a letter from the city, cancelling the ticket.
Word got around. People started coming at odd hours.
A teenager bought C3 for a dollar and got, sorry I said your drawings were childish.
It was from his older brother, who had moved away two years before, and who, that same evening,
called for the first time in months.
A retired schoolteacher bought D5 and got an apology from a student she had failed in nineteen eighty-one, who,
it turned out, had become a schoolteacher too. The cheap ones were small and specific.
The expensive ones were not. Nobody bought F6 for a long time.
Eleven dollars and forty cents is a strange amount, and people were nervous about what that much sorry would contain.
Petrosyan watched all of this from the little office by the entrance. He didn't buy anything.
He told himself it was because he was the manager, and it would be unprofessional.
On a Sunday in February, when the garage was nearly empty,
a man in a grey suit fed in a ten-dollar bill and a fistful of coins and pressed F6.
The machine hummed for a long time.
When the envelope finally dropped, it was thicker than the others.
The man opened it, read it standing up,
and then sat down on the concrete floor and stayed there for almost an hour.
Petrosyan brought him a coffee. Neither of them said anything about what was in the envelope.
The man left the paper on the floor when he went.
Petrosyan picked it up to throw it away, and he did not mean to read it,
but it was only one line. It said, sorry, this one is from you.
In March, the machine was gone.
There was a clean rectangle on the floor where the dust hadn't settled, and nothing else.
Petrosyan still works there.
Every morning he walks past the empty spot between the stairwell and the broken elevator,
and every morning he thinks about calling his sister. Some mornings, now, he does.
That's the story. Thanks for listening.
